title: Nearly 30% of American Car Buyers Are Rolling Record Debt Into New Vehicles
excerpt: Average negative equity on trade-ins hit $6,884 in Q2 2026, as pandemic-era buyers return to dealerships carrying thousands in underwater loans amid elevated interest rates.
body:
• Nearly 30% of new-vehicle trade-ins in Q2 2026 carried negative equity, the highest second-quarter share since 2020, with average underwater balances reaching a record $6,884.
  • Monthly payments for buyers rolling over negative equity averaged $944, compared to the industry-wide average of $777, as a record 23.9% of borrowers signed 84-month-or-longer loans.
  • Pandemic-era buyers who financed at 2022 peak prices are now returning to dealerships, creating a compounding debt cycle that industry analysts call a "costly snowball effect."
  • The Chevrolet Silverado 1500, Ford F-150, and Ram 1500 top the list of vehicles with the highest average negative equity, each exceeding $8,300.

A Debt Cycle Accelerates at the Dealership

Americans are financing new cars under increasingly punishing terms, with nearly three in ten trade-ins now carrying more debt than the vehicle is worth, according to new data from Edmunds released this week.

The average negative equity on underwater trade-ins reached $6,884 in the second quarter of 2026, up from $6,754 a year earlier and a record for any second quarter in Edmunds’ tracking history. The share of trade-ins in a negative-equity position climbed to 29.6%, up from 26.6% in Q2 2025.

"Consumers are incurring more debt than ever when trading in vehicles that are underwater. Buyers who financed at 2022’s peak prices are starting to come back to trade in, and they’re bringing thousands of dollars in old debt with them."

— Jessica Caldwell, Head of Insights, Edmunds

Pandemic Hangover Meets Elevated Rates

The roots of the current crisis trace back to 2022, when a semiconductor shortage and supply-chain disruptions left dealer lots bare. Buyers paid at or above sticker price for whatever was available, often adding extended warranties and dealer-installed options that inflated loan balances.

Four years later, those vehicles have depreciated sharply while the original loan balances remain stubbornly high. When owners return to trade in, they discover they owe thousands more than their car is worth—and many roll that shortfall into a new, larger loan.

Ivan Drury, Edmunds’ director of insights, described the dynamic bluntly: "They should be ahead but they’re not." He noted that even vehicles with traditionally strong resale values, such as the Toyota Tacoma, are showing up with average negative equity of $7,793 because of punishing original loan terms.

Bigger Loans, Longer Terms, Higher Payments

The industry’s response to sticker shock has been to stretch loan terms ever further. A record 36.5% of buyers who financed a new vehicle in Q2 2026 opted for loans of 73 months or longer, up from 27.3% a decade ago. Nearly one in four—23.9%—signed loans of at least 84 months, or seven years.

Average monthly payments hit a new record of $777 across all new-vehicle loans. For those rolling over negative equity, payments surged to $944 per month, and the average amount financed ran about $11,000 higher than the typical buyer’s.

With average new-vehicle transaction prices hovering near $50,000 and interest rates around 7%, the math is unforgiving. A $40,000 loan at 7% over seven years still carries a balance of roughly $25,200 after three years of on-time payments.

Which Vehicles Carry the Most Debt

Full-size pickup trucks dominate the list of models with the deepest negative equity. The Chevrolet Silverado 1500 leads at $8,516 on average, followed by the Ford F-150 at $8,417 and the Ram 1500 at $8,347. Popular sedans and SUVs also appear: the Toyota Camry at $7,030, the Nissan Rogue at $7,260, and the Toyota Corolla at $6,191.

A Warning for NRI Buyers

For members of the Indian diaspora settled in the United States—many of whom purchased vehicles during the 2022 shortage—the data carries a specific caution. Financial advisors recommend checking your payoff balance against your car’s current market value before visiting a dealership. Shopping for pre-approved auto loans from credit unions or online lenders, rather than relying solely on dealer financing, can also reduce the risk of rolling old debt into a new purchase.

What Comes Next

Industry observers expect negative equity to remain elevated through the rest of 2026. Subprime auto-loan delinquencies are already running near 30-year highs, with the 60-day delinquency rate hitting a record 6.9% in January 2026, according to Fitch Ratings. The Federal Trade Commission, meanwhile, has targeted roughly 100 dealership groups for deceptive pricing practices, including mandatory fees not reflected in advertised prices.

The question for consumers is whether the cycle breaks before the next wave of trade-ins. For now, the data suggests it is only deepening.
nri_angle: Indian Americans who bought vehicles during the 2022 shortage may be carrying significant negative equity and should check loan balances against current market values before trading in.
author: Diaspora Desk
